items.title: The best model for early product validation is almost never the best model for production
items.text: The best model for early product validation is almost never the best model for production. Talked to a bunch of founders this weekend. There’s a standard playbook emerging : 1/ Prototype with the best frontier models. Max quality. Ignore cost and latency. Learn what users actually want and iterate. 2/ Once the workflow and UX is validated, optimize like crazy for cost and latency - prompt eng, model routing, harnesses, smaller models, fine tuning. I see most teams get stuck in step 1.

items.text: Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:22 One of our big guiding principles is just simplicity. So, like, when you look at a model like, let's say, CHI one, I think there are 23 distinct submodules in CHI one. And, like, when you're trying to iterate on something like that, it gets really hard because you're like, I kinda I need to understand each of these sub modules independently. I need to understand all of their behaviors, their dynamics, and, like, that doesn't actually scale that well. So, like, you can start to think, okay. Speaker 1 | 00:22 - 00:31 How do I simplify this? How do I identify, like, what's what's really important? Once you have that, the whole research process and identifying these types of scaling directions becomes a lot simpler. items.text: Contrary to popular perception, most people will not adopt a new technology just because it makes them more efficient. Instead, they’ll adopt new technology because: - Someone they know who’s similar to them on some dimension adopted the technology, and got positive results (eg became cooler, richer, more popular/respected), and they wanna become like that person - They feel like everyone around them has adopted the technology, and if they don’t, they’ll be left behind Notice that it’s not entirely a rational decision.
